title: Building Production REST APIs with Django REST Framework
subtitle: Structuring ViewSets, auto-routing, Swagger docs, fan-out HTTP calls, background threads, and schedulers in Python Django.
overview: Django REST Framework (DRF) is the gold standard for building RESTful APIs in Python. This article walks through the patterns that make a DRF project production-ready: using ViewSets with DefaultRouter to auto-wire CRUD routes, overriding action methods for custom logic, making fan-out HTTP calls to upstream services and merging their responses, using Enums to centralise endpoint configuration, auto-generating OpenAPI/Swagger documentation with drf-yasg, and running background work with Django AppConfig, threading, APScheduler, and Celery.
problem: Raw Django views require a lot of repetitive glue: manually wiring every URL, writing the same create/read/update/delete logic for every resource, maintaining separate Swagger YAML files that drift out of sync with the code, and hand-rolling thread management for background jobs. DRF solves the first two. drf-yasg solves the third. AppConfig hooks and task queues solve the fourth.
architecture: The project follows standard Django project layout with a single app (`main`). Routing is handled by DRF's `DefaultRouter`, which registers a `ModelViewSet` and emits all six standard routes automatically. The ViewSet overrides the `list` action to fan out to two external APIs, merges the responses on a shared key, and returns a unified payload. Endpoint URLs live in a Python `Enum` so they are never scattered across business logic. Swagger UI is mounted at `/doc/` via `drf_yasg` and reflects the live schema with no manual maintenance.

implementation.title: Project setup and dependencies
implementation.description: Install Django, DRF, drf-yasg for Swagger, and requests for outbound HTTP calls. Use a virtual environment to isolate dependencies.
implementation.code:
# requirements.txt
django==4.1
djangorestframework==3.10.3
drf-yasg==1.20.0
requests==2.31.0

# Install
pip install -r requirements.txt

# settings.py — register the apps
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    'rest_framework',
    'drf_yasg',
    'main',          # your app
]

implementation.title: DefaultRouter — six routes, zero boilerplate
implementation.description: Registering a ViewSet with `DefaultRouter` automatically creates GET /items/, POST /items/, GET /items/{id}/, PUT /items/{id}/, PATCH /items/{id}/, and DELETE /items/{id}/. No manual `path()` calls needed per route.
implementation.code:
# main/urls.py
from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter
from .views import MockItemViewSet

router = DefaultRouter()
router.register(r'items', MockItemViewSet, basename='items')

urlpatterns = router.urls

# djangoAPI/urls.py  (project-level)
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    path('', include('main.urls')),
    # swagger and admin registered separately
]

implementation.title: Enum-based endpoint configuration
implementation.description: Hard-coding URLs inside business logic makes tests brittle and configuration changes painful. An `Enum` centralises all external endpoint URLs in one place, making them easy to override with environment variables or a config file.
implementation.code:
# main/enum.py
from enum import Enum
import os

class MockEndpointsEnum(Enum):
    ORDERS_API   = os.getenv('ORDERS_API_URL',   'https://mock.api/orders')
    PRODUCTS_API = os.getenv('PRODUCTS_API_URL',  'https://mock.api/products')

# Usage in views
url = MockEndpointsEnum.ORDERS_API.value

implementation.title: Fan-out HTTP calls and response merging
implementation.description: A common pattern is to call multiple upstream services and join their responses on a shared key before returning to the client. The ViewSet overrides `list()` to do exactly this — two requests fire sequentially (or can be parallelised with `concurrent.futures`), then the responses are zipped on `customer_id`.

implementation.title: Parallel fan-out with concurrent.futures
implementation.description: When the two upstream calls are independent, fire them in parallel using a `ThreadPoolExecutor`. This halves latency when each call takes similar time.

implementation.title: Auto-generated Swagger / OpenAPI docs with drf-yasg
implementation.description: drf-yasg introspects your ViewSets and serializers at startup and generates a live OpenAPI 2.0 schema — no YAML files to maintain. Mount the Swagger UI and ReDoc at separate URLs.
implementation.code:
# djangoAPI/urls.py
from drf_yasg.views import get_schema_view
from drf_yasg import openapi
from rest_framework import permissions
from django.urls import path

schema_view = get_schema_view(
    openapi.Info(
        title='Items API',
        default_version='v1',
        description='Auto-generated API documentation',
        contact=openapi.Contact(email='you@example.com'),
    ),
    public=True,
    permission_classes=(permissions.AllowAny,),
)

urlpatterns = [
    # Swagger UI
    path('doc/', schema_view.with_ui('swagger', cache_timeout=0), name='schema-swagger-ui'),
    # ReDoc (alternative clean reader)
    path('redoc/', schema_view.with_ui('redoc', cache_timeout=0), name='schema-redoc'),
    # Raw JSON schema
    path('swagger.json', schema_view.without_ui(cache_timeout=0), name='schema-json'),
]

implementation.title: Background threads via AppConfig.ready()
implementation.description: Django's `AppConfig.ready()` fires once after the app registry is fully loaded — the right place to start a long-running background thread without blocking the request cycle. Use a daemon thread so it exits when the main process exits.

implementation.title: Periodic scheduling with APScheduler
implementation.description: For more structured scheduling (cron expressions, intervals, job stores), embed APScheduler directly in Django. The `BlockingScheduler` runs in a dedicated thread started from `AppConfig.ready()`.
implementation.code:
# pip install apscheduler

# main/scheduler.py
from apscheduler.schedulers.background import BackgroundScheduler
from apscheduler.triggers.cron import CronTrigger
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def sync_data():
    logger.info('Running scheduled sync...')
    # call external APIs, update DB, etc.

def start():
    scheduler = BackgroundScheduler()
    # Run sync_data every day at 02:00
    scheduler.add_job(
        sync_data,
        trigger=CronTrigger(hour=2, minute=0),
        id='sync_data',
        replace_existing=True,
    )
    scheduler.start()
    logger.info('APScheduler started')

# main/apps.py — call from ready()
from main import scheduler

class MainConfig(AppConfig):
    name = 'main'
    def ready(self):
        scheduler.start()

implementation.title: Distributed task queues with Celery + Redis
implementation.description: For production workloads — retries, rate-limiting, fan-out at scale — replace in-process threads with Celery. Tasks are pushed to a Redis broker and consumed by separate worker processes, making them resilient to web dyno restarts.
implementation.code:
# pip install celery[redis]

# djangoAPI/celery.py
import os
from celery import Celery

os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'djangoAPI.settings')

app = Celery('djangoAPI')
app.config_from_object('django.conf:settings', namespace='CELERY')
app.autodiscover_tasks()

# settings.py
CELERY_BROKER_URL = 'redis://localhost:6379/0'
CELERY_RESULT_BACKEND = 'redis://localhost:6379/0'

# main/tasks.py
from celery import shared_task
from celery.utils.log import get_task_logger

logger = get_task_logger(__name__)

@shared_task(bind=True, max_retries=3, default_retry_delay=30)
def process_item(self, item_id: int):
    try:
        logger.info('Processing item %s', item_id)
        # ... do work ...
    except Exception as exc:
        raise self.retry(exc=exc)

# Dispatch from a view
from .tasks import process_item
process_item.delay(item_id=42)

# Run worker
# celery -A djangoAPI worker --loglevel=info

# Celery Beat for periodic tasks
# celery -A djangoAPI beat --loglevel=info

implementation.title: Structured logging and error handling
implementation.description: Centralise logging config in settings.py. Use `logging.getLogger(__name__)` in every module so log records carry the module path. Always return meaningful HTTP status codes from DRF views — never swallow exceptions silently.

impact: Six CRUD routes registered with a single `router.register()` call — zero per-route boilerplate
Swagger UI live at /doc/ with no annotation overhead — schema reflects code automatically
Fan-out to multiple upstream APIs merged into one clean response payload
Background threads and scheduled jobs decoupled from the request lifecycle via AppConfig.ready()
Celery + Redis pattern scales background workload horizontally across worker processes
lessons: DefaultRouter is the fastest path from a ViewSet to a full REST surface — register once, get all six verbs
Enum for endpoint configuration prevents URL literals from scattering across business logic and makes environment-specific overrides trivial
drf-yasg requires zero annotations for basic schemas — introspection covers 80% of real-world APIs out of the box
The RUN_MAIN guard in AppConfig.ready() is essential — Django's development server spawns two processes and the guard prevents double-starting background threads
For anything beyond simple periodic pings, Celery is the right answer: it gives you retries, rate limiting, task visibility, and horizontal scaling that threading.Thread cannot
